background:
Colossians: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes

Study notes · dates are approximate and scholars vary

At a glance

Colossians is Paul's portrait of Christ as supreme over all creation, written to a church he had never visited, threatened by a teaching that added rules, rituals and spiritual powers to Christ. It was sent with Ephesians and Philemon around AD 60–62.

QuestionTraditional viewNotes
AuthorPaul, with Timothy (1:1)Traditionally Paul; some scholars think a close follower wrote it in his name. It closely parallels Ephesians.
Date and placeAbout AD 60–62, from prison, probably in RomeSome suggest an earlier imprisonment in Ephesus, much closer to Colossae.
RecipientsThe church at Colossae, a small city in the Lycus valleyPaul had not visited; Epaphras, a Colossian, founded the church (1:7; 4:12).
Carried byTychicus, with Onesimus (4:7–9)Onesimus was the runaway slave Paul sent back to Philemon, a member of this church.
Companion lettersEphesians and Philemon; a letter “from Laodicea” (4:16)The Laodicean letter is lost, unless it is Ephesians.
The problemA “philosophy” mixing Jewish rules, worship of angels and self-denial (2:8–23)Paul answers that believers have everything “in him,” for in Christ “dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (2:9).

Colossians has two halves: who Christ is and what He has done (1–2), and how believers live because they have been raised with Him (3–4).

Paul's life and the writing of Colossians

Dates are approximate. Colossians is one of four “prison letters,” with Ephesians, Philippians and Philemon.

Approx. dateEventScripture

Rome and the province of Asia

Paul wrote from Rome in Nero's reign to a small city in one of the empire's richest provinces.

  • Paul in chains. Paul was under house arrest in Rome, guarded by soldiers, with friends like Luke, Mark, Aristarchus and Epaphras around him (4:10–14).
  • A rich province. Asia was wealthy from trade, textiles and banking. Its cities competed for the honor of building temples to the emperors.
  • The earthquake. Tacitus says Laodicea was destroyed by an earthquake in AD 60 and rebuilt from its own resources without help from Rome. Colossae, ten miles away, was probably damaged too.
  • Slavery. Slaves were everywhere in Roman households. Colossians gives instructions to slaves and masters (3:22–4:1) while sending a runaway slave, Onesimus, home as “the faithful and beloved brother” (4:9).
  • Philosophies and mystery cults. The region was full of teachers offering secret knowledge and initiation rites. Paul uses some of their language (“fulness,” “mystery,” “perfect”) to show that all of it is found in Christ.
  • Triumphs. When Rome celebrated a victory, defeated rulers were paraded through the streets. Paul says Christ did this to the spiritual “principalities and the powers” at the cross (2:15).

Writing near the empire's capital, Paul declares that every throne and dominion was created by Christ and for Him (1:16).

Colossae and the Lycus valley

Colossae sat in the Lycus River valley, about 120 miles east of Ephesus on the main road to the east.

  • Colossae. Once a large city on the Persian royal road, by Paul's day it had been overtaken by its neighbors. It was known for wool dyed a deep red color named after the city.
  • Laodicea. Ten miles west, a wealthy banking and textile center, later rebuked in Revelation as “lukewarm” (Rev 3:14–22).
  • Hierapolis. Six miles north of Laodicea, famous for hot springs that left white mineral terraces, and for a cave of poisonous gas called the Plutonium.
  • Epaphras. A native of Colossae who probably heard Paul in Ephesus and planted churches in all three cities (1:7; 4:12–13).
  • Jews in the valley. In 62 BC a Roman governor seized about 20 pounds of gold collected by Jews at Laodicea for the Jerusalem temple, a sign of a large Jewish community. That may explain the stress on Sabbaths, new moons and food laws (2:16).
  • Philemon's house. The church in Colossae met at least partly in the home of Philemon, Apphia and Archippus (Phlm 1–2; Col 4:17).

The time map

The shaded band marks AD 60–62. Tacitus records a great earthquake at Laodicea, Colossae's neighbor, in AD 60.

Around the world in AD 60–62

Colossians was written in a dramatic period for the Roman world.

RegionWhat was happening
BritainBoudica's revolt (AD 60–61). The queen of the Iceni burned London, Colchester and St Albans before being crushed.
RomeNero's early good years ended about AD 62. The Great Fire of AD 64 was followed by the first persecution of Christians.
JudeaTension grew; James the Lord's brother was killed in AD 62. The Jewish revolt broke out in AD 66.
Armenia and ParthiaA compromise peace in AD 63; Nero crowned the Parthian prince Tiridates king of Armenia in Rome in AD 66.
ItalyAn earthquake damaged Pompeii and Herculaneum in AD 62, seventeen years before Vesuvius buried them.
ChinaThe Eastern Han dynasty under Emperor Ming; silk reached Rome along the trade routes.
IndiaThe Kushan Empire was forming in the northwest; tradition says Thomas preached in India.
The AmericasTeotihuacan was growing; the Moche and Nazca cultures flourished in Peru.

Maps: then and now

Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis lay close together in the Lycus valley, along the road from Ephesus to the east. A traveler could walk between them in an afternoon.

Today the Colossae mound near Honaz has never been fully excavated, though work began recently. Laodicea and Hierapolis (Pamukkale) are major archaeological sites near Denizli.

How the setting shapes the study

Colossians uses images its readers in the Lycus valley would recognize.

PassageConnection to the times
Col 1:15–20In a world full of thrones and powers, including the emperor, Paul says all things were created through Christ and for Him.
Col 1:26–27Mystery cults offered secrets to initiates; Paul's “mystery” is Christ in you, revealed to all.
Col 2:8“Philosophy and vain deceit”: traveling teachers offered competing systems.
Col 2:14“The bond written in ordinances” is a handwritten certificate of debt, canceled by being nailed to the cross.
Col 2:15In a Roman triumph, defeated enemies were paraded publicly.
Col 2:16A large Jewish community in the valley kept feasts, new moons and Sabbaths.
Col 3:11Scythians, from north of the Black Sea, were Greeks' byword for the most uncivilized barbarians.
Col 3:22–4:1Onesimus, a runaway slave, was traveling with this letter (4:9).
Col 4:16Letters were copied and passed between churches; this one was to be read in Laodicea too.

Against teachers who offered more, Paul's answer is that in Christ “ye are made full” (2:10).

items.text: Greeting, Thanksgiving and Prayer
Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Timothy our brother,
to the saints and faithful brethren in Christ that are at Colossæ: Grace to you and peace from God our Father.
We give thanks to God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, praying always for you,
having heard of your faith in Christ Jesus, and of the love which ye have toward all the saints,
because of the hope which is laid up for you in the heavens, whereof ye heard before in the word of the truth of the gospel,
which is come unto you; even as it is also in all the world bearing fruit and increasing, as it doth in you also, since the day ye heard and knew the grace of God in truth;
even as ye learned of Epaphras our beloved fellow-servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ on our behalf,
who also declared unto us your love in the Spirit.
For this cause we also, since the day we heard it, do not cease to pray and make request for you, that ye may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding,
to walk worthily of the Lord unto all pleasing, bearing fruit in every good work, and increasing in the knowledge of God;
strengthened with all power, according to the might of his glory, unto all patience and longsuffering with joy;
giving thanks unto the Father, who made us meet to be partakers of the inheritance of the saints in light;
who delivered us out of the power of darkness, and translated us into the kingdom of the Son of his love;
in whom we have our redemption, the forgiveness of our sins:
The Supremacy of Christ
who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation;

for in him were all things created, in the heavens and upon the earth, things visible and things invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things have been created through him, and unto him;
and he is before all things, and in him all things consist.
And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.
For it was the good pleasure of the Father that in him should all the fulness dwell;
and through him to reconcile all things unto himself, having made peace through the blood of his cross; through him, I say, whether things upon the earth, or things in the heavens.
And you, being in time past alienated and enemies in your mind in your evil works,
yet now hath he reconciled in the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and without blemish and unreproveable before him:

if so be that ye continue in the faith, grounded and stedfast, and not moved away from the hope of the gospel which ye heard, which was preached in all creation under heaven; whereof I Paul was made a minister.
Paul's Ministry to the Church
Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake, and fill up on my part that which is lacking of the afflictions of Christ in my flesh for his body’s sake, which is the church;
whereof I was made a minister, according to the dispensation of God which was given me to you-ward, to fulfil the word of God,
even the mystery which hath been hid for ages and generations: but now hath it been manifested to his saints,
to whom God was pleased to make known what is the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory:
whom we proclaim, admonishing every man and teaching every man in all wisdom, that we may present every man perfect in Christ;
whereunto I labor also, striving according to his working, which worketh in me mightily.

summary.title: CHAPTER 1 IN SUMMARY
paras: Paul and Timothy thank God for the Colossians' faith in Christ, their love for all the saints and their hope laid up in heaven, which they heard in the gospel from Epaphras. Paul prays that they will be filled with the knowledge of God's will, walk worthily of the Lord and bear fruit, giving thanks to the Father, who “delivered us out of the power of darkness, and translated us into the kingdom of the Son of his love.” Then comes a great hymn to Christ: He is “the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation,” through whom and for whom all things were created, including thrones and authorities. He is before all things, holds all things together, and is the head of the church. In Him all the fullness dwells, and through His blood on the cross God reconciled all things to Himself. Paul rejoices to suffer for the church and labors to present everyone mature in Christ, proclaiming the mystery: “Christ in you, the hope of glory.”

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: List the claims made about Christ in verses 15–20; what do they say about his relation to creation, the church and reconciliation?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: For a young church in Colossae, founded through Epaphras (v. 7) rather than Paul, why would hearing of the gospel bearing fruit everywhere be reassuring?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: Paul prays for knowledge that leads to a worthy walk (vv. 9–12); how could you shape your own prayers for others around these requests?

items.text: Paul's Concern for the Churches
For I would have you know how greatly I strive for you, and for them at Laodicea, and for as many as have not seen my face in the flesh;
that their hearts may be comforted, they being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, that they may know the mystery of God, even Christ,
in whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden.
This I say, that no one may delude you with persuasiveness of speech.
For though I am absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit, joying and beholding your order, and the stedfastness of your faith in Christ.
As therefore ye received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him,
rooted and builded up in him, and established in your faith, even as ye were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.
Alive in Christ
Take heed lest there shall be any one that maketh spoil of you through his philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ:
for in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily,
and in him ye are made full, who is the head of all principality and power:
in whom ye were also circumcised with a circumcision not made with hands, in the putting off of the body of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ;
having been buried with him in baptism, wherein ye were also raised with him through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead.
And you, being dead through your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, you, I say, did he make alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses;
having blotted out the bond written in ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us: and he hath taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross;
having despoiled the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it.
Let No One Disqualify You
Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of a feast day or a new moon or a sabbath day:
which are a shadow of the things to come; but the body is Christ’s.
Let no man rob you of your prize by a voluntary humility and worshipping of the angels, dwelling in the things which he hath seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind,
and not holding fast the Head, from whom all the body, being supplied and knit together through the joints and bands, increaseth with the increase of God.
If ye died with Christ from the rudiments of the world, why, as though living in the world, do ye subject yourselves to ordinances,
Handle not, nor taste, nor touch
(all which things are to perish with the using), after the precepts and doctrines of men?
Which things have indeed a show of wisdom in will-worship, and humility, and severity to the body; but are not of any value against the indulgence of the flesh.

summary.title: CHAPTER 2 IN SUMMARY
paras: Paul struggles in prayer for believers in Colossae and Laodicea who have never seen him, that they may know Christ, “in whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden.” He warns them not to be deluded by persuasive talk, but to walk in Christ as they received Him, rooted, built up and abounding in thanksgiving.

Let no one take them captive through philosophy and empty deceit based on human tradition, for in Christ all the fullness of deity dwells bodily, and in Him they are made full. They were spiritually circumcised and buried and raised with Him in baptism; God forgave their sins, canceled the record of debt by nailing it to the cross, and disarmed the powers, triumphing over them. So no one should judge them over food, festivals or Sabbaths, which were shadows of Christ, or disqualify them by insisting on angel worship and visions. Such man-made rules look wise but have no value against indulging the flesh.

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: What does Paul say God did with the bond written against us in verses 13–15, and how does he describe Christ's victory over powers?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: Why would rules about food, festivals, new moons and sabbaths (vv. 16–23) have appealed to believers in Colossae seeking extra spiritual security?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: Which rules, practices or experiences do people today add to Christ as a test of real spirituality, and how might verses 8–10 speak to them?

items.text: Put On the New Self
If then ye were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God.
Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth.
For ye died, and your life is hid with Christ in God.
When Christ, who is our life, shall be manifested, then shall ye also with him be manifested in glory.
Put to death therefore your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry;
for which things’ sake cometh the wrath of God upon the sons of disobedience:
wherein ye also once walked, when ye lived in these things;
but now do ye also put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, railing, shameful speaking out of your mouth:
lie not one to another; seeing that ye have put off the old man with his doings,
and have put on the new man, that is being renewed unto knowledge after the image of him that created him:
where there cannot be Greek and Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, barbarian, Scythian, bondman, freeman; but Christ is all, and in all.
Put on therefore, as God’s elect, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, meekness, longsuffering;
forbearing one another, and forgiving each other, if any man have a complaint against any; even as the Lord forgave you, so also do ye:
and above all these things put on love, which is the bond of perfectness.
And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to the which also ye were called in one body; and be ye thankful.
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; in all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another with psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts unto God.
And whatsoever ye do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
Wives and Husbands, Children and Fathers, Servants 3:18–
Wives, be in subjection to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.
Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them.
Children, obey your parents in all things, for this is well-pleasing in the Lord.
Fathers, provoke not your children, that they be not discouraged.
Servants, obey in all things them that are your masters according to the flesh; not with eye-service, as men-pleasers, but in singleness of heart, fearing the Lord:
whatsoever ye do, work heartily, as unto the Lord, and not unto men;
knowing that from the Lord ye shall receive the recompense of the inheritance: ye serve the Lord Christ.
For he that doeth wrong shall receive again for the wrong that he hath done: and there is no respect of persons.

summary.title: CHAPTER 3 IN SUMMARY
paras: Since they have been raised with Christ, believers should seek the things above, where Christ is, and set their minds there, for their life is hidden with Christ in God. They must put to death what is earthly in them (immorality, impurity, evil desire, covetousness) and put away anger, malice, slander and lying, having put off the old man and put on the new, in which there is neither Greek nor Jew, barbarian, Scythian, slave or free, “but Christ is all, and in all.”

As God's chosen ones, they should put on compassion, kindness, humility, meekness and patience, forgiving one another as the Lord forgave them, and above all love. Let the peace of Christ rule in their hearts and His word dwell in them richly, “And whatsoever ye do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus.” Paul then gives instructions to households: wives and husbands, children and fathers, and servants, who are to work heartily “as unto the Lord,” for they serve the Lord Christ.

questions.label: NOW

items.text: Masters; Prayer and Wise Speech
Masters, render unto your servants that which is just and equal; knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven.
Continue stedfastly in prayer, watching therein with thanksgiving;
withal praying for us also, that God may open unto us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also in bonds;
that I may make it manifest, as I ought to speak.
Walk in wisdom toward them that are without, redeeming the time.
Let your speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer each one.
Final Greetings
All my affairs shall Tychicus make known unto you, the beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow-servant in the Lord:
whom I have sent unto you for this very purpose, that ye may know our state, and that he may comfort your hearts;
together with Onesimus, the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They shall make known unto you all things that are done here.
Aristarchus my fellow-prisoner saluteth you, and Mark, the cousin of Barnabas (touching whom ye received commandments; if he come unto you, receive him),
and Jesus that is called Justus, who are of the circumcision: these only are my fellow-workers unto the kingdom of God, men that have been a comfort unto me.
Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, saluteth you, always striving for you in his prayers, that ye may stand perfect and fully assured in all the will of God.
For I bear him witness, that he hath much labor for you, and for them in Laodicea, and for them in Hierapolis.
Luke, the beloved physician, and Demas salute you.
Salute the brethren that are in Laodicea, and Nymphas, and the church that is in their house.
And when this epistle hath been read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans; and that ye also read the epistle from Laodicea.
And say to Archippus, Take heed to the ministry which thou hast received in the Lord, that thou fulfil it.
The salutation of me Paul with mine own hand. Remember my bonds. Grace be with you.

summary.title: CHAPTER 4 IN SUMMARY
paras: Masters must treat their servants justly and fairly, knowing that they too have a Master in heaven. Paul asks the Colossians to continue steadfastly in prayer with thanksgiving, praying for an open door for the gospel, and to walk in wisdom toward outsiders, their speech always gracious, “seasoned with salt.”

Tychicus and Onesimus will tell them all about Paul. Greetings come from Aristarchus, Mark (Barnabas' cousin), Jesus called Justus, Epaphras, who labors in prayer for them, Luke the beloved physician, and Demas. They should greet the believers in Laodicea and Nympha and the church in her house, exchange letters with Laodicea, and tell Archippus to fulfill his ministry. Paul signs with his own hand: “Remember my bonds. Grace be with you.”

questions.label: NOW

wrap.title: Colossians In Summary
paras: Colossians is a letter about the supremacy and sufficiency of Christ. Some teachers in Colossae were offering a “philosophy” that added special knowledge, angel worship, food rules, festivals and harsh self-denial to faith in Christ, as if believers needed something more. Paul answers that they need nothing more, because they have Christ.

The heart of the letter is the hymn in 1:15–20. Christ is the image of the invisible God and the firstborn over all creation; everything in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, including thrones and powers, was created through Him and for Him. He holds all things together, He is the head of the church, and through His blood on the cross God reconciled all things to Himself.

Because “in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (2:9), believers “are made full” in Him. At the cross God forgave their sins, canceled the record of their debt and triumphed over the spiritual powers. Rules about food and festivals were only shadows; the reality is Christ. Human regulations cannot change the heart.

Chapters 3–4 show the new life that follows. Believers have been raised with Christ, so they set their minds on things above, put off the old ways and put on compassion, kindness, forgiveness and love. In Christ the barriers between Greek and Jew, barbarian and Scythian, slave and free are gone. Ordinary life at home and work becomes service to the Lord.

The letter closes with warm greetings to a church Paul had never seen, carried by Tychicus and a returning slave, Onesimus. The message in one line: Christ is Lord over all creation and all powers, and in Him believers have everything they need, so they should live their whole lives for Him.
